question: An insecticide of the neonicotinoid family, thiacloprid is used to kill aphids or Colorado beetles in fruit and vegetable crops, particularly beetroot. It was banned throughout the European Union in 2020 because of its impact on pollinators and because it is considered to be reprotoxic, an endocrine disruptor and probably carcinogenic to humans.

However, it is still used in third countries, which then export fruit and vegetables containing thiacloprid residues to the EU. This trade therefore constitutes unfair competition against our own farmers, who are subject to stricter and more costly health and environmental rules.

In response to the legitimate anger of farmers, the French Prime Minister recently announced a ban on imports into France of products treated with thiacloprid. Other Member States are expected to commit to similar measures in the near future.

To help them meet their promise, will the Commission propose a reform to improve checks on compliance with maximum residue limits for plant protection products in imports, as current border controls are too often limited to checking certificates issued only by the authorities of exporting countries?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.4.2024) The Commission would like to clarify that the reasons for the non-renewal of the approval of thiacloprid1 were its classification as toxic for reproduction category 1B in accordance with Regulation (EC) 1272/20082 and its potential for contamination of groundwater above the parametric value of 0.1 microgram per liter (µg/l) for pesticides in drinking water3.

Member States are responsible for carrying out controls and ensuring that food placed on the market is safe, regardless of its origin. Through an EU-coordinated multi-annual control programme4 and further risk-based national control programmes5, Member States monitor compliance with Maximum Residues Levels of pesticides6, both for domestic production and imports.
According to the monitoring results from the 2021 EFSA report for thiacloprid, from the total 65851 samples analysed only nine have values above the legal limit7.

Where a risk of contamination of products imported from a third country is identified, including in particular for active substances prohibited in the EU, the Commission may amend measures under Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/17938 requiring reinforced import checks at border control posts at harmonised frequencies and certification by the exporting country.

By regularly introducing amendments to the Annexes of that Regulation the Commission ensures that controls on commodities imported from third countries remain risk-based, in order to safeguard the health of the citizens in the EU.
